messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi had been working late at his clinic when the attack happened, a normal evening of notes, a half-finished cup of tea, and the familiar responsibility of being the calm one in the room. He was 37, married, and had spent years helping other people make sense of fear, which made the terror of that night feel especially violating to him. The bombing and the gunfire that followed shattered the street outside his office, and what stayed with him most was the sudden loss of control: the sound of shots cracking through the dark, people screaming, his own body freezing while he tried to decide whether to run or hide. In the weeks after, night-time became charged with the memory of that helplessness. Waking in the dark would jolt him upright, heart racing, and any sharp bang—especially a noise that resembled a gunshot—would pull him back to the scene with immediate force. Those moments did not just frighten him; they seemed to confirm what he had already begun to believe, that he could not stop bad things from happening to him and that the world was, at its core, dangerous.

As those triggers became part of daily life, Ravi started arranging his life around them. He avoided anything that could be stressful, turning down work that felt emotionally demanding, leaving tasks undone, and shrinking his world to the safest routines he could manage. At night he kept the lights on longer than he used to, and when sleep came he preferred to drift off into a world of his own rather than remain with the images that surfaced in the dark. On some evenings he drank, or took medication more readily than before, or used whatever would dull the edges enough to get through the night. He told himself these were temporary measures, but they slowly became the main way he kept going. The more he let fear set the terms, the more convinced he became that he was no longer recognisable to himself. The steady, thoughtful man he had once assumed himself to be felt replaced by someone tense, avoidant, and altered in ways he did not know how to explain to his wife.

That sense of being changed fed back into his behaviour. Ravi found himself thinking that if he could not keep catastrophe away, he had to at least keep it from reaching him emotionally, and so he retreated further from difficult conversations, busy schedules, and anything that might unsettle him. When the stress of managing work, sleep, and his own vigilance built up, he reached for the same numbing strategies again, not because they solved anything but because they offered brief relief from the thought that his mind and body had become unreliable. Yet the more he relied on them, the less confident he felt, and the more the world seemed dangerous and unpredictable. He started scanning for risk even in places that should have felt familiar, and that constant alertness made the nighttime and the slightest sudden noise feel even more potent than before.

The cost of this pattern was visible at work and at home. As a psychologist, Ravi could still perform the basics, but he had begun declining fuller caseloads and avoiding sessions that might bring up trauma, grief, or crisis. He was present in the office, yet psychologically elsewhere at times, drifting into private mental worlds to get through moments he did not trust himself to handle. His wife noticed that he was more distant and less available in the evenings, and he felt ashamed that the person he had become seemed so unlike the one she married. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the constant effort of keeping himself away from stress, darkness, and sudden sound, and by the sense that every attempt to cope had only confirmed his helplessness. What brought him in was the growing fear that he could not continue living so narrowly, and what he most hoped for was to feel like himself again without waiting for the next shock in the dark.
